```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r model-load, include = FALSE}
mod_bic <- readModelDb("Oliveira_2026_bictegravir_rabbit")
mod_isl <- readModelDb("Oliveira_2026_islatravir_rabbit")
mod_ftc <- readModelDb("Oliveira_2026_emtricitabine_rabbit")
ui_bic <- rxode2::rxode(mod_bic)
ui_isl <- rxode2::rxode(mod_isl)
ui_ftc <- rxode2::rxode(mod_ftc)

# Typical-value versions. The bictegravir and islatravir models carry
# zero-variance etas (variances not reported); the naive-pooled emtricitabine
# model has no etas, so only its residual error is zeroed.
typ <- list(
  bictegravir = rxode2::zeroRe(ui_bic),
  islatravir = rxode2::zeroRe(ui_isl),
  emtricitabine = rxode2::zeroRe(ui_ftc, which = "sigma")
)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r ui_bic$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics18050522>
* Supplement (Figures S1-S7; Table S1, absorption-model estimates; Table S2,
  absorption-vs-dissolution models):
  <https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/pharmaceutics18050522/s1>

Oliveira and colleagues developed a biodegradable, reservoir-style
poly(caprolactone) implant that is placed subcutaneously and releases one of
three antiretrovirals: bictegravir (BIC), islatravir (ISL) or emtricitabine
(FTC). The intended use is long-acting HIV treatment for children aged 2 to 5
years. In New Zealand White rabbits they:

1. fitted a two-compartment macro-constant model (A, alpha, B, beta) to sparse
   plasma concentrations after a single IV bolus of each drug (Table 3);
2. used the dose-normalised biexponential as the unit impulse response to
   deconvolve each implant's subcutaneous absorption rate over one year
   (Table 4, Figure 4);
3. fitted dissolution models to the median fraction absorbed over time; the
   best were a Weibull model for BIC and double-Weibull models for ISL and FTC
   (Supplementary Table S1);
4. translated the deconvolved absorption rates into predicted paediatric
   steady-state concentrations, `Css = k0 / CL`, with published clinical
   clearances (Tables 1 and 4).

The three drugs were fitted separately, so the package has one model per drug:

* `Oliveira_2026_bictegravir_rabbit`: `r ui_bic$description`
* `Oliveira_2026_islatravir_rabbit`: `r ui_isl$description`
* `Oliveira_2026_emtricitabine_rabbit`: `r ui_ftc$description`

Each model has the IV disposition (dose into `central`) and the implant
absorption (dose into `depot`, and also into `depot2` for the double-Weibull
drugs). Doses are per kg of body weight because the IV doses were given per kg
and the paper reports no rabbit body weights.

# Population

Twenty-four New Zealand White rabbits received a single IV bolus into the
marginal ear vein, 8 per group: BIC 0.75 mg/kg alone, ISL/FTC 5/30 mg/kg, or
BIC/ISL/FTC 0.75/5/30 mg/kg (Methods, In Vivo Absorption; Supplementary
Figure S1). Sampling was sparse: two samples per rabbit at 0.5, 1, 3, 6, 12,
18, 24 or 30 h, giving four observations per group per time. Sixteen rabbits
therefore informed each drug's IV model. For FTC, five rabbits whose
observations were all below the limit of quantification were omitted, leaving
11.

After a 7-week washout the same rabbits received subcutaneous implants placed
between the scapulae: two BIC implants (BIC-only group), one ISL plus one FTC
implant, or one of each. Mean loaded masses were 165 mg (BIC), 62 mg (ISL) and
100 mg (FTC) per implant. Each group had equal numbers of males and females.
Two rabbits per group were necropsied at 3 and at 6 months. The BIC-only group
stopped at day 56; the other groups were followed for one year.

```{r population}
str(ui_isl$population)
```

# IV disposition

## Closed-form check

The ODE model must reproduce the paper's biexponential exactly:
`C(t) = A exp(-alpha t) + B exp(-beta t)` after the reference dose.

```{r iv-sim}
paper_times <- c(0.5, 1, 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30)
iv_ref <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~dref, ~A, ~alpha, ~B, ~beta,
  "bictegravir", 0.75, 1115.6, 0.438, 102.0, 0.170,
  "islatravir", 5, 5275.9, 0.45, 6.3, 0.06,
  "emtricitabine", 30, 25323.5, 0.64, 810.5, 0.13
)

iv_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 30, by = 0.25), paper_times)))
sim_iv <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(iv_ref)), function(i) {
  r <- iv_ref[i, ]
  ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    data.frame(id = i, time = 0, evid = 1, amt = r$dref, cmt = "central"),
    data.frame(id = i, time = iv_grid, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
  )
  out <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(typ[[r$drug]], ev, returnType = "data.frame"))
  # A single-subject solve returns no id column.
  out$id <- i
  out$drug <- r$drug
  out
}))

closed <- sim_iv |>
  dplyr::select(drug, time, Cc) |>
  dplyr::left_join(iv_ref, by = "drug") |>
  dplyr::mutate(Cc_closed = A * exp(-alpha * time) + B * exp(-beta * time),
                rel_err = abs(Cc / Cc_closed - 1))
closed |>
  dplyr::group_by(drug) |>
  dplyr::summarise(max_rel_err = max(rel_err)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 8)
# Same parameters on both sides: the difference is pure solver error.
stopifnot(max(closed$rel_err) < 1e-4)
```

## Figure 3A-C: mean IV profiles

The solid line in Figure 3A-C is the model's population prediction at the
sampling times. It passes through the printed BIC estimates exactly, for
example ln C = 2.95 at 12 h. For ISL and FTC the paper prints the final alpha
and beta to one decimal place only. The maintainers read the line off
Figure 3 (to about +/- 0.15 ln units) and compared it with two candidates.
The first uses the printed one-decimal values. The second uses the bootstrap
medians from the same table (0.45 and 0.06 for ISL; 0.64 and 0.13 for FTC),
which lie inside the rounding intervals of the printed values. The packaged
models use the bootstrap medians, together with the final A and B.

```{r fig3-iv}
fig3_digitised <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~time, ~lnC,
  "bictegravir", 0.5, 6.85, "bictegravir", 1, 6.65, "bictegravir", 3, 5.95,
  "bictegravir", 6, 4.75, "bictegravir", 12, 2.95, "bictegravir", 18, 1.65,
  "bictegravir", 24, 0.6, "bictegravir", 30, -0.45,
  "islatravir", 0.5, 8.4, "islatravir", 1, 8.2, "islatravir", 3, 7.2,
  "islatravir", 6, 5.9, "islatravir", 12, 3.35, "islatravir", 18, 1.3,
  "islatravir", 24, 0.4, "islatravir", 30, 0.0,
  "emtricitabine", 0.5, 9.85, "emtricitabine", 1, 9.55, "emtricitabine", 3, 8.6,
  "emtricitabine", 6, 6.75, "emtricitabine", 12, 5.2, "emtricitabine", 18, 4.3,
  "emtricitabine", 24, 3.5, "emtricitabine", 30, 2.7
)

rounded <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~A, ~alpha, ~B, ~beta,
  "islatravir", 5275.9, 0.5, 6.3, 0.1,
  "emtricitabine", 25323.5, 0.6, 810.5, 0.1
)
rounded_curve <- merge(rounded, data.frame(time = iv_grid)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lnC = log(A * exp(-alpha * time) + B * exp(-beta * time)),
                source = "Table 3 final estimates as printed (1 decimal)")

model_curve <- sim_iv |>
  dplyr::transmute(drug, time, lnC = log(Cc), source = "Packaged model")

ggplot(dplyr::bind_rows(model_curve, rounded_curve),
       aes(time, lnC, linetype = source)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig3_digitised, aes(time, lnC), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~drug, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "ln plasma concentration (ng/mL)", linetype = NULL,
       caption = "Red points: Figure 3A-C population-prediction line, read by the maintainers.") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Replicates Figure 3A-C of Oliveira 2026.

```{r fig3-check}
fit_check <- fig3_digitised |>
  dplyr::left_join(model_curve |> dplyr::select(drug, time, lnC_model = lnC),
                   by = c("drug", "time")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(rounded_curve |> dplyr::select(drug, time, lnC_rounded = lnC),
                   by = c("drug", "time")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(diff_model = lnC_model - lnC, diff_rounded = lnC_rounded - lnC)

fit_check |>
  dplyr::group_by(drug) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `max |model - Figure 3|` = max(abs(diff_model)),
    `max |printed 1-decimal - Figure 3|` = max(abs(diff_rounded))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

# The packaged models stay within reading error of the published line; the
# printed one-decimal ISL and FTC rate constants miss it by about 1 ln unit at
# 30 h. The model and the line share the same parameters, so the remaining
# difference is reading error from the figure.
stopifnot(
  max(abs(fit_check$diff_model)) < 0.3,
  all(abs(fit_check$diff_rounded[fit_check$time == 30 &
                                    fit_check$drug != "bictegravir"]) > 0.9)
)
```

## PKNCA: IV terminal slope

Table 2 reports the terminal slope (lambda-z) from a sparse NCA of the
observed IV data over 0-30 h. The model's NCA uses the same sampling times.

```{r iv-nca}
iv_nca_in <- sim_iv |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc), time %in% c(0, paper_times)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(treatment = drug) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, treatment)

iv_dose <- iv_ref |>
  dplyr::transmute(id = seq_len(dplyr::n()), time = 0, amt = dref, treatment = drug)

iv_conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(iv_nca_in, Cc ~ time | treatment + id,
                                concu = "ng/mL", timeu = "h")
iv_dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(iv_dose, amt ~ time | treatment + id, doseu = "mg/kg")
iv_nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  iv_conc_obj, iv_dose_obj,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, cmax = TRUE, lambda.z = TRUE,
                         half.life = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE)
))

published_iv <- tibble::tribble(
  ~treatment, ~lambda.z,
  "bictegravir", 0.181,
  "islatravir", 0.216,
  "emtricitabine", 0.154
)
knitr::kable(
  nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
    simulated = iv_nca,
    reference = published_iv,
    by = "treatment",
    units = c(lambda.z = "1/h"),
    tolerance_pct = 20
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Typical-value NCA vs. Oliveira 2026 Table 2 IV bolus lambda-z.",
    "* differs from reference by >20%."
  )
)
```

BIC and FTC agree within 20%. ISL does not, and the reason is the shape of
its profile rather than a model error. The ISL beta phase carries only 0.1% of
the IV curve (B = 6.3 against A = 5275.9 ng/mL) and emerges only over the last
sampling times. Between 18 and 30 h the model's slope is about 0.11 1/h
(Figure 3B). PKNCA's best-fit point selection instead takes the steeper
alpha-dominated points and returns 0.30 1/h. The paper's 0.216 1/h, from an
NCA of the observed sparse data, lies between the two. Over 0-30 h the
ISL lambda-z depends on which points are used, so it is not a sharp check.

# Implant absorption

## Fraction of the loaded mass remaining

The Results state the percentage of loaded mass expected to remain in the
implant at 6 and 12 months: 81 and 65% (BIC), 48 and 45% (ISL), 49 and 36%
(FTC). The model reproduces these figures from its depot amounts. Each
implant dose here is the mean loaded mass per kg for an illustrative 4 kg
rabbit. Fractions do not depend on the weight chosen.

```{r implant-sim}
implant <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~load_mg, ~cmts,
  "bictegravir", 165, list("depot"),
  "islatravir", 62, list(c("depot", "depot2")),
  "emtricitabine", 100, list(c("depot", "depot2"))
)
wt_illustrative <- 4 # kg; rabbit body weights are not reported
day_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 371, by = 1), 182.5, 365)))

sim_imp <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(implant)), function(i) {
  r <- implant[i, ]
  dose <- r$load_mg / wt_illustrative
  ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    data.frame(id = i, time = 0, evid = 1, amt = dose, cmt = unlist(r$cmts)),
    data.frame(id = i, time = day_grid * 24, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
  )
  out <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(typ[[r$drug]], ev, returnType = "data.frame"))
  if (!"depot2" %in% names(out)) out$depot2 <- 0
  fdep <- exp(typ[[r$drug]]$theta[["lfdepot"]])
  out |>
    dplyr::mutate(drug = r$drug, load_mg = r$load_mg, dose = dose,
                  absorbed_frac = (fdep * dose - depot - depot2) / dose,
                  day = time / 24)
}))

remaining <- sim_imp |>
  dplyr::filter(day %in% c(182.5, 365)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(drug, month = ifelse(day == 365, 12, 6),
                   model_pct = 100 * (1 - absorbed_frac)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(tibble::tribble(
    ~drug, ~month, ~paper_pct,
    "bictegravir", 6, 81, "bictegravir", 12, 65,
    "islatravir", 6, 48, "islatravir", 12, 45,
    "emtricitabine", 6, 49, "emtricitabine", 12, 36
  ), by = c("drug", "month"))
remaining |>
  dplyr::rename(Drug = drug, Month = month,
                `Model remaining (%)` = model_pct,
                `Paper remaining (%)` = paper_pct) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)

# The Weibull fits and the paper's percentages are the same curves, so the
# differences are rounding, except FTC at 12 months (see text).
stopifnot(
  median(abs(remaining$model_pct - remaining$paper_pct)) < 1,
  max(abs(remaining$model_pct - remaining$paper_pct)) < 3.5
)
```

Five of the six values agree to within 1 percentage point. FTC at 12 months
differs by about 3 points (38.9 against 36%). That difference comes from the
published double-Weibull fit itself: Finf = 0.614 caps absorption at 61% of
the load, so at least 38.6% always remains.

The model's depot release must also equal the analytic Weibull fraction
absorbed:

```{r weibull-identity}
weibull_F <- function(drug, t) {
  p <- typ[[drug]]$theta
  finf <- exp(p[["lfdepot"]])
  s1 <- exp(-(exp(p[["lra"]]) * t)^exp(p[["lgam1"]]))
  if (drug == "bictegravir") {
    finf * (1 - s1)
  } else {
    f1 <- plogis(p[["logitfrel"]])
    s2 <- exp(-(exp(p[["lra2"]]) * t)^exp(p[["lgam2"]]))
    finf * (f1 * (1 - s1) + (1 - f1) * (1 - s2))
  }
}
ident <- sim_imp |>
  dplyr::filter(day > 0) |>
  dplyr::group_by(drug) |>
  dplyr::mutate(F_analytic = weibull_F(dplyr::first(drug), time)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(max(abs(ident$absorbed_frac - ident$F_analytic)) < 1e-4)
```

## Figure 4: absorption rate and cumulative mass

The model's absorption rate is the loaded mass times `dF/dt`, here for an
implant with the mean loaded mass. Points are the deconvolved medians of
Table 4.

```{r fig4}
rate <- sim_imp |>
  dplyr::group_by(drug) |>
  dplyr::arrange(day, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cum_mg = absorbed_frac * load_mg,
    rate_ug_day = 1000 * (cum_mg - dplyr::lag(cum_mg)) / (day - dplyr::lag(day))
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::filter(day >= 1)

table4 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~month, ~rate_ug_day, ~cum_mg, ~css_paper,
  "bictegravir", 1, 172.5, 5.5, 43.0,
  "bictegravir", 3, 116.0, 11.8, 28.9,
  "bictegravir", 6, 97.6, 20.5, 24.4,
  "bictegravir", 12, 70.9, 37.7, 17.7,
  "islatravir", 1, 294.8, 11.2, 1.09,
  "islatravir", 3, 116.0, 23.5, 0.43,
  "islatravir", 6, 37.4, 31.5, 0.14,
  "islatravir", 12, 4.7, 34.3, 0.02,
  "emtricitabine", 1, 420.5, 18.1, 2.4,
  "emtricitabine", 3, 236.2, 36.8, 1.3,
  "emtricitabine", 6, 116.6, 50.1, 0.7,
  "emtricitabine", 12, 24.1, 67.8, 0.1
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(day = month * 365 / 12)

ggplot(rate, aes(day, rate_ug_day, colour = drug)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = table4) +
  labs(x = "Time after implantation (day)", y = "Absorption rate (ug/day)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

ggplot(rate, aes(day, cum_mg, colour = drug)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = table4) +
  labs(x = "Time after implantation (day)", y = "Cumulative mass absorbed (mg)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

Replicates Figure 4A and 4B of Oliveira 2026 (model lines; Table 4 medians as
points).

```{r table4-compare}
rate_at <- rate |>
  dplyr::select(drug, day, model_rate = rate_ug_day, model_cum = cum_mg)
cmp4 <- table4 |>
  dplyr::mutate(day = round(day)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(rate_at, by = c("drug", "day"))
cmp4 |>
  dplyr::select(drug, month, rate_ug_day, model_rate, cum_mg, model_cum) |>
  dplyr::rename(Drug = drug, Month = month,
                `Table 4 rate (ug/day)` = rate_ug_day,
                `Model rate (ug/day)` = model_rate,
                `Table 4 cumulative (mg)` = cum_mg,
                `Model cumulative (mg)` = model_cum) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

For ISL and FTC the cumulative mass agrees with Table 4 to within about 10%
over the year, and the rates agree over the first 6 months. At 12 months the
model rates are lower (ISL 0.7 against 4.7 ug/day; FTC 8 against 24 ug/day).
The double-Weibull fits level off at Finf, while the deconvolved medians
still show some absorption. For BIC the model's cumulative mass at 12
months (about 58 mg) exceeds the Table 4 median (37.7 mg). The model and the
table rest on different subsets of rabbits. The Weibull curve was fitted to
the median fraction absorbed of the rabbits followed for the whole year (n = 4
at 12 months for BIC); the Results' 65% remaining at 12 months comes from that
same curve. Table 4 is the median over the rabbits present at each time
(n = 8 at the start), in mg rather than as a fraction of each rabbit's load. The
model reproduces the fraction curve, which is what the paper fitted; converting
it back to mg with the mean load of all BIC implants is approximate.

## Plasma concentrations from an implant (Figure 3D-F)

Plasma concentrations from an implant depend on body weight. Rabbit weights
are not reported, so this illustration uses 4 kg. It should match Figure 3D-F
in level and shape, not point by point.

```{r fig3-sq}
ggplot(dplyr::filter(sim_imp, day >= 1), aes(day, Cc)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~drug) +
  labs(x = "Time after implantation (day)", y = "Plasma concentration (ng/mL)",
       caption = "Typical rabbit of 4 kg (illustrative) with one implant of the mean loaded mass.") +
  theme_bw()
```

Compare with Figure 3D-F of Oliveira 2026. Concentrations are about 5-15 ng/mL
BIC over the year, 1-10 ng/mL ISL falling steeply after about 6 months, and
2-10 ng/mL FTC declining through the year.

# Paediatric translation (Tables 1 and 4)

The paper predicts paediatric steady-state concentrations as `Css = k0 / CL`.
Here `k0` is the deconvolved rabbit absorption rate and `CL` is the clinical
clearance in Table 1. BIC: 30 mg x 0.70 / 126 ug h/mL = 167 mL/h. FTC:
120 mg x 0.93 / 15 ug h/mL = 7440 mL/h. ISL: adult CL/F = 35,860 mL/h scaled
by `(15/70)^0.75` = 11,294 mL/h. The table below recomputes the Table 4
column, first from the Table 4 rates and then from the model rates. The
model-rate column inherits the differences discussed under Figure 4; in
particular, the BIC model rates sit above the Table 4 medians.

```{r peds}
cl_ped <- c(
  bictegravir = 30 * 0.70 / 126 * 1000,
  emtricitabine = 120 * 0.93 / 15 * 1000,
  islatravir = 35860 * (15 / 70)^0.75
)
stopifnot(
  abs(cl_ped[["bictegravir"]] - 167) < 0.5,
  abs(cl_ped[["emtricitabine"]] - 7440) < 0.5,
  abs(cl_ped[["islatravir"]] - 11294) < 1
)
peds <- cmp4 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cl_ml_h = cl_ped[drug],
    css_from_table4 = rate_ug_day * 1000 / 24 / cl_ml_h,
    css_from_model = model_rate * 1000 / 24 / cl_ml_h
  )
peds |>
  dplyr::select(drug, month, css_paper, css_from_table4, css_from_model) |>
  dplyr::rename(Drug = drug, Month = month,
                `Table 4 Css (ng/mL)` = css_paper,
                `Recomputed from Table 4 rate` = css_from_table4,
                `From model rate` = css_from_model) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
# The paper's arithmetic is reproduced to its printed rounding.
stopifnot(all(abs(peds$css_from_table4 - peds$css_paper) <
                pmax(0.05, 0.02 * peds$css_paper)))
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **ISL and FTC rate constants.** Table 3 prints the final alpha and beta for
  ISL (0.5, 0.1 1/h) and FTC (0.6, 0.1 1/h) to one decimal place. With the
  final A and B, those values miss the published population-prediction line
  of Figure 3B-C by about 1 ln unit at 30 h. The bootstrap medians in the same
  table (ISL 0.45 and 0.06; FTC 0.64 and 0.13) lie inside the rounding
  intervals and reproduce the line to within reading error. The packaged
  models use the bootstrap medians for these four rate constants and the
  final estimates for every other value. BIC is printed to three significant
  figures and uses the final estimates throughout.
* **Dosing per kg.** The IV doses were per kg and the paper reports no rabbit
  body weights, so the models take doses in mg/kg and volumes in L/kg. An
  implant loaded with M mg in a rabbit of W kg is a dose of M / W mg/kg. The
  4 kg weight used for the implant plasma illustration is the maintainers'
  choice; it does not enter any check.
* **Between-animal variability and residual error.** The BIC and ISL models
  had random effects on A, alpha, B and beta, but their variances are not
  reported. The etas on alpha and beta are kept as `fixed(0)`. The etas on A
  and B have no one-to-one counterpart on `vc` and `k21` and are not carried.
  The FTC model was naive-pooled and has no etas. The log-additive residual
  error is encoded as `lnorm(expSd)` with `expSd` fixed to 0 because its
  magnitude is not reported. Simulations are therefore typical-value only.
* **Implant input.** The implant absorption is the published Weibull or
  double-Weibull fit to the *median* fraction absorbed (Table S1). It is a
  typical-implant description, not an individual-level model, and it is valid
  over the one year it was fitted to. For BIC, Finf = 1.67 exceeds 1 because
  the fit spans only the first 35% of release. Extrapolated far beyond a year,
  the BIC model would absorb more than the loaded mass.
* **Weibull time origin.** The release hazard of BIC (shape 0.949 < 1) is not
  finite at the moment of implantation. The time after the implant dose is
  floored at 1e-6 h, which changes the absorbed amount by a negligible
  fraction. A cap at a cumulative hazard of 40 stops a shape above 1 from
  growing without bound after a depot is empty.
* **Double-Weibull pairing.** Phoenix Model 603 pairs F1 with the first
  process (MDT1, b1). Pairing F1 with the second process instead would leave
  53% of the FTC load at 6 months, against the paper's 49%. The pairing used
  here gives 49.9%.
* **Not encoded.** Two parts of the paper are not packaged as models. The
  absorption-vs-dissolution regressions (Table S2, Figure 5) are statistical
  regressions of in vivo fraction absorbed on in vitro fraction dissolved,
  and need an in vitro dissolution curve as input. The paediatric `Css`
  translation is reproduced above as arithmetic. The alternative dissolution
  models of Table S1 (zero-order, first-order, Higuchi, Makoid-Banakar) were
  not selected and are not packaged.
* **Errata.** No erratum or correction was found for this article (checked
  2026-11-13).
